About CMN S3(AE)
1. About CMN S3(AE)
The CMN S3(AE) is a scalable and conﬁgurable coherent AMBA®5 CHI interconnect designed
to meet the Power, Performance, and Area (PPA) requirements for Coherent Mesh Network
systems that are used in high-end networking, enterprise compute, and server class automotive
applications.
CMN S3(AE) is a scalable mesh interconnect with 1-256 processor compute clusters.
CMN S3(AE) is conﬁgurable with the Arm® Socrates™ IP Tooling platform. The Arm® Socrates™ IP
Tooling platform is an environment for the conﬁguration of Arm IP. Using Arm®Socrates™ IP Tooling
platform, you can conﬁgure the following CMN S3(AE) characteristics:
•
Custom interconnect size and device placement.
•
Optional System Level Cache (SLC). For more information about the features of the SLC
memory system, see SLC memory system.
For more information on conﬁguring the Arm® Socrates™ IP Tooling platform, see the Arm®
Socrates™ User Guide.
CMN S3(AE) supports Arm® AMBA® CHI Architecture Speciﬁcation
CMN S3(AE) provides system-level alignment by providing the following system functionality:
•
Quality of Service (QoS)
•
Reliability, Availability, and Serviceability (RAS)
•
Debug and Trace (DT)
CMN S3(AE) is compatible with the following types of IP:
•
Dynamic Memory Controller (DMC)
•
Generic Interrupt Controller (GIC)
•
Memory Management Unit (MMU)
•
Interconnects such as the Arm® CoreLink™ NIC-450 Network Interconnect
•
Armv8.2, Armv8.4, Armv9.0, and Armv9.2 processors
CMN S3(AE) provides an optional Coherent Multichip Link (CML) feature. CML is compliant with:
•
CXL 2.0 and CXL 3.0 standard for memory expansion and Type 1 accelerators
•
CML_SMP connection for both 64B and 256B ﬂit formats
•
C2C I/O coherent support speciﬁed in AMBA® CHI Chip-to-Chip (C2C) Architecture Speciﬁcation
CMN S3(AE) is made up of various types of protocol nodes and devices. The following table shows
the protocol nodes and devices that a system that is built using CMN S3(AE) can contain:

® Neoverse™ CMN S3(AE) Coherent Mesh Network

Issue 05
About CMN S3(AE)
Table 1-1: Supported protocol nodes and devices
Protocol node or device
Description
Fully coherent
Requesting Node (RN-F)
A fully coherent Requester device that supports:
•
CHI Issue B
•
CHI Issue C
•
CHI Issue D
•
CHI Issue E
•
CHI Issue F
•
CHI Issue G
I/O coherent Requesting
Node (RN-I)
An I/O-coherent Requester device. This CHI bridge device acts as an RN-I proxy for one or more AXI or ACE-
Lite Requester devices that connect to it.
I/O coherent Requesting
Node with DVM support
(RN-D)
An I/O coherent Requester device that supports acceptance of Distributed Virtual Memory (DVM) messages
on the Snoop channel
Fully coherent Home
Node (HN-F)
A device that acts as a Home Node for a coherent region of memory. HN-Fs accept coherent requests from
RN-Fs and RN-Is, and generates snoops to all applicable RN-Fs in the system as required to support the
coherency protocol.
Super Home Node (HN-
S)
A device that acts as a Fully coherent Home Node (HN-F) for a local coherent memory region and acts as a
Local Coherency Node (LCN) for a remote coherent memory region.
I/O coherent Home
Node (HN-I)
A device that acts as a Home Node for the Completer I/O subsystem, responsible for ensuring proper ordering
of requests targeting the Completer I/O subsystem. HN-I supports AMBA® AXI and ACE-Lite protocols.
I/O coherent Home
Node + DVM Node (HN-
D)
A device that includes an HN-I, a Debug Trace Controller (DTC), DVM Node (DN), conﬁguration node (CFG),
Global Conﬁguration Completer, and the Power/Clock Control Block (PCCB). HN-D supports the AMBA® AXI,
ACE-Lite, ATB, and APB protocols.
Note:
Only one HN-D is allowed per CMN S3(AE) instance.
I/O coherent Home
Node + DTC (HN-T)
An HN-I with a built-in DTC, DN, and ATB. HN-T supports the AMBA® AXI and ACE-Lite protocols.
I/O coherent Home
Node + Distributed DVM
Node (HN-V)
A device that includes an HN-I and DN. HN-V supports the AMBA® AXI and ACE-Lite protocols.
I/O coherent
Home Node + PCIe
optimization (HN-P)
A device that includes HN-I and dedicated trackers for PCIe peer-to-peer traﬃc. This device can only be used
to connect to PCIe Completers. HN-P supports the AMBA® AXI and ACE-Lite protocols.
CHI Completer Node
(SN-F)
A device which solely receives CHI commands, limited to fulﬁlling simple read, write, and CMO requests
targeting normal memory
AMBA®5 CHI to ACE5-
Lite bridge SBSX
A CHI bridge device that converts and forwards simple CHI read, write, and CMO commands to an AXI or
ACE-Lite Completer memory device. Device ordering is not maintained in SBSX.
CXL Gateway (CCG)
A CCG device bridges between CHI and CXS Issue B through a CML_SMP or CXL port, or a C2C port.

1.1 Compliance
The CMN S3(AE) product is based on Issue G of the AMBA® CHI Architecture Speciﬁcation.
This Technical Reference Manual (TRM) complements Architecture Reference Manuals, architecture
speciﬁcations, protocol speciﬁcations, and relevant external standards. It does not duplicate
information from these sources.
AMBA® CHI architecture
CMN S3(AE) supports a subset of the AMBA® CHI Architecture Speciﬁcation Issue G, and is also
backwards compatible with Issue F, Issue E, Issue D, Issue C, and Issue B. For more information
about compatibility see Backward compatible RN-F support.
CMN S3(AE) implements the following architecture capabilities:
•
Fully compliant with CHI interconnect architecture
•
Non-blocking coherence protocol
•
Packet-based communication
The following four types of channels:
•
Request (REQ)
•
Response (RSP)
•
Snoop (SNP)
•
Data (DAT)
•
Credited end-to-end protocol-layer ﬂow-control with a retry once mechanism for ﬂexible
bandwidth and resource allocation
•
Integrated end-to-end Quality-of-Service (QoS) capabilities
See the AMBA® CHI Architecture Speciﬁcation for more information.
CXL architecture
CMN S3(AE) supports CXL.mem (Type3) and CXL.cache (Type 1) functionality for host
implementation and is compliant with Compute Express Link (CXL) speciﬁcation revision 2.0 dated
October 2020 and CXL 3 revision 3.0 version 1.0 release candidate dated June 2022.
1.2 Features
CMN S3(AE) provides the following key features:
•
Highly scalable mesh network topology conﬁgurable up to a 12 x 12 mesh
•
Custom mesh size and device placement
•
A programmable System Address Map (SAM)

1.4 Conﬁgurable options
The basic structure of CMN S3(AE) is a conﬁgurable rectangular grid that is composed of network
routers that are known as Crosspoints (XPs) and CHI-compliant devices.
Each XP connects horizontally and vertically to other XPs, creating a two-dimensional mesh
structure. In a mesh conﬁguration, each XP can have up to four device ports for connecting CHI-
compliant devices. See Crosspoint.
CMN S3(AE) provides several conﬁgurable parameters that can be conﬁgured to meet system
requirements. You can use Arm® Socrates™ IP Tooling platform to reﬁne the mesh design and
device placement using the following guidelines. For more information on conﬁguring the Arm®
Socrates™ IP Tooling platform, see the Arm® Socrates™ User Guide.
CMN S3(AE) is conﬁgured using the following steps:
1.
System component selection. In this step, system components are determined, including:

1.4.1 System component selection
This following describes CMN S3(AE) system component selection.
Request Nodes
Request Nodes (RNs) reside outside of the mesh and connect to CMN S3(AE) ports.
Requesters with coherent caches, which includes processors, GPUs, or processing elements with
internal coherent caches, are referred to as RN-F devices. They connect directly to the CMN
S3(AE) interconnect mesh using a CHI RN-F port.
I/O requesters without coherent caches connect to CMN S3(AE) RN-I bridge devices using ACE-
Lite ports or CMN S3(AE) RN-D bridge devices using ACE-Lite-with-DVM ports. Examples of I/O
requesters include DMA controllers, PCIe controllers, processing elements without internal caches,
or processing elements with internal caches that are not hardware coherent. The RN-I and RN-D
bridge device is located between the ACE-Lite interface and the internal CHI interface. Each RN-I
or RN-D bridge device has up to three ACE-Lite interfaces.
A single I/O requester can be connected directly to a CMN S3(AE) ACE-Lite port. Alternatively,
multiple requesters can share a single ACE-Lite port by connecting through external AMBA®
interconnect components. To determine if I/O requesters share 1-3 ACE-Lite ports or an RN-I,
designers must consider traﬃc bandwidth requirements and physical ﬂoorplan trade-oﬀs.
Copyright © 2023–2025 Arm Limited (or its aﬃliates). All rights reserved.
Non-Conﬁdential

Arm
® Neoverse™ CMN S3(AE) Coherent Mesh Network
Technical Reference Manual
Document ID: 107858_0203_05_en
Issue 05
About CMN S3(AE)
Home Nodes
In CHI, each byte of address space is assigned to a single Home Node (HN). That HN is responsible
for handling all memory transactions that are associated with that address.
There are three types of HN devices within the CMN S3(AE) system:
HN-F
HN-F device instances are the Home Nodes for all coherent memory. HN-Fs also support
non-coherent memory accesses. Memory that is mapped to an HN-F targets DRAM. Each
HN-F can contain an SF and an optional SLC slice. The amount of SLC required determines
the number of HN-Fs. The total SLC size required divided by the number of HN-F instances
determines the recommended SLC size for each HN-F instance. Generally, each HN-F
partition has the same SLC size. You must conﬁgure the amount of SLCs and number of HN-
Fs separately.
The optimal total SF size is twice the total exclusive cache size for all local RN-
Fs. For example, for a 32MB local RN-F total cache size, the recommended SF
size is 64MB.
HN-S
In this book any descriptions related to the Fully coherent Home Node (HN-F)
also apply to the Super Home Node (HN-S).
HN-S device instances, act as HN-F nodes for local coherent memory and Local Coherency
Nodes (LCNs) for remote coherent memory. HN-S also support non-coherent memory
accesses for local memory. Memory that is mapped to HN-S targets local and remote DRAM.
Each HN-S can contain an SF and an SLC, both shared between HN bound traﬃc (HBT) and
LCN bound traﬃc (LBT). For more information about partitioning the SLC between HBT and
LBT lines, see HN-S SLC and LCC capacity partitioning.
The amount of SLC required determines the number of HN-Ss. The total SLC size required
divided by the number of HN-S instances determines the recommended SLC size for each
HN-S instance. Generally, each HN-S partition has the same SLC size. The amount of SLC
and number of HN-S nodes are conﬁgured separately.
The optimal total SF size is twice the total exclusive cache size for all RN-
Fs and total LCC size on remote chips. For example, for a 32MB RN-F total
cache size and a 16MB total LCC cache size, the recommended SF size is
96MB.
Copyright © 2023–2025 Arm Limited (or its aﬃliates). All rights reserved.

HN-I
HN-I device instances are the HNs for all memory that targets an ACE-Lite completer device
or subsystem. HN-I does not support coherent memory. However, Cacheable transactions
can be sent to HN-I. Each HN-I instance contains a single ACE-Lite requester port to send
bus transactions to one or more completers through an AMBA® interconnect. The total ACE-
Lite requester bandwidth requirement, and physical placement of completer peripherals,
determines the number of HN-I instances that are required. Cacheable transactions to HN-I
are downgraded to WriteNoSnoop and ReadNoSnoop when issuing to ACE-Lite. By default,
a RAS error is generated as described in section HN-I error handling unless disabled via HN-
I’s cfg_ctl.reqerr_cohreq_en bit, described in section HN-I register summary. There are HN-I
types with extra functionality. These types include:
HN-T
HN-I that has a debug trace controller and DVM Node. CMN S3(AE) can have zero or
more HN-I and HN-T instances.
HN-D
HN-I that has a debug trace controller, DVM Node, and conﬁguration Completer. CMN
S3(AE) must have exactly one HN-D instance.
HN-P
HN-I that is optimized for peer-to-peer PCIe traﬃc.
HN-V
A device that includes an HN-I and DVM Node (DN).
CML interfaces
The CMN S3(AE) interconnect supports up to 32 CXS (CXL/CML_SMP/CHI C2C) interfaces. Each
CCG device has a CXS interface, which is compliant with CXS Issue B speciﬁcation.
A CCG device bridges between CHI and CXS, and contains Request Agent (RA) proxy and Home
Agent (HA) proxy functionality. The CCG device also contains CXS Link Agent (LA) functionality,
which implements CML_SMP, CXL, or CHI C2C ﬂits.
Memory interfaces
The CMN S3(AE) interconnect supports the following types of memory interface ports:
CHI SN-F port
Connects a native CHI memory controller that complies with:
•
CHI Issue C
•
CHI Issue D
•
CHI Issue E
•
CHI Issue F
•
CHI Issue G
ACE-Lite port
Connects an AXI or ACE-Lite memory controllers to CMN S3(AE) through an ACE-Lite
memory interface on one of the following node types:

SBSX
SBSXs bridge between CHI and ACE-Lite protocols. Each SBSX has a single ACE-Lite
interface.
MTSX
MTSXs also bridge CHI and ACE-Lite protocols, and each MTSX has a single ACE-Lite
interface. However, MTSX are only instantiated when the system requires MTE support
but the subordinate AXI or ACE-Lite memory controller does not support MTE.
SBSX and MTSX support both Direct Memory Transfers (DMT) and Direct
Subordinate Access (DSA). If the AXI data bus size is 128-bits, the downstream AXI
target must not interleave beats of read data at less than a 32 byte boundary.
The number and type of memory interfaces that you require depends on the design of your
system. For more information, see Mesh sizing and top-level conﬁguration.
1.4.2 Mesh sizing and top-level conﬁguration
The size of the CMN S3(AE) mesh primarily depends on the number of connected devices.
The product of the X and Y mesh dimensions must be greater than or equal to the required number
of XPs. For example, if seven XPs are required, a 2 x 4 or 4 x 2 mesh would be acceptable.

1.4.3 Device placement and conﬁguration
When the devices are enumerated and the mesh dimensions are determined, the placement of
each device or node in the mesh must be speciﬁed.
While there are no constraints on the mesh location of a device, ﬂoor-planning and performance
constraints drive the optimal device placement. This detail is outside the scope of this document.
The following table shows the options that you can use to conﬁgure individual CMN S3(AE)
devices.
When CAL, except HCAL, is present, all the devices that are connected to it must
be conﬁgured identically.
Table 1-7: CHI device conﬁgurable options: RN-F port, SN-F port
Parameter
Description
Values
(Default)
Comments
DATACHECK_EN Datacheck
enable
0, 1 (0)
End-to-end data byte parity enable applicable to SN-F or RN-F* when global
datacheck is enabled

WR_GATHER_PRESENT
Builds the
HN-P Write
Gathering
buﬀer
0, 1 (1)
If set, the write gathering logic is built into HN-P. The other HNx do not support this
feature.
WR_GATHER_NUM_BUF
Number
of Write
Gathering
buﬀers.
2-6 (4)
Chooses the number of write gathering buﬀers to instantiate. Ideally this would be
set to >= the number of unique P2P write streams seen by HN-P, where a stream is
identiﬁed by the requesting RN-I’s or RN-D’s Chip ID, logical ID, AXI port number, and
hashed AWID. RN-I and RN-D uses a 4-bit hash to map the incoming AXI AWID to a
4-bit hashed value sent with the write over CHI.
WR_GATHER_BUF_SIZE Size of
Write
Gathering
buﬀers.
0, 1 (1)
Determines the size of the write data buﬀer in bytes. This should be set to <= PCIe
Maximum Payload Size (MPS). If MPS > this parameter, the a gathered burst will be
sent out when the buﬀer has ﬁlled. For the values described 0 = 256 bytes and 1 =
512 bytes.

1.5 Test features
The CMN S3(AE) product includes several test features.
For information about the test features see the Arm® Neoverse™ CMN S3(AE) Coherent Mesh
Network Conﬁguration and Integration Manual.
1.6 Product documentation and design ﬂow
The CMN S3(AE) product books support the design ﬂow process.
These documents do not reproduce information that is available in the Arm architecture and
protocol speciﬁcations. For architecture and protocol information that relates to CMN S3(AE), see
Useful resources on page 2184.
Documentation
The CMN S3(AE) product is supported by the following documentation:
Technical Reference Manual
The Technical Reference Manual (TRM) describes the functionality, and how functional
options aﬀect the behavior of CMN S3(AE). It is required at all stages of the design ﬂow. The
choices that you make in the design ﬂow can mean that some behavior that is described in
the TRM is not relevant. If you are programming the CMN S3(AE) product, contact:
•
The implementer to determine:
◦
The build conﬁguration of the implementation
◦
What integration, if any, was performed before implementing the CMN S3(AE) product
•
The integrator to determine the pin conﬁguration of the device that you are using
Conﬁguration and Integration Manual
The Conﬁguration and Integration Manual (CIM) describes how to integrate the CMN S3(AE)
product into an SoC. It includes a description of the pins that the integrator must tie oﬀ to
conﬁgure the macrocell for the required integration. The CIM also describes:
•
The available build conﬁguration options and related issues in selecting them
•
How to conﬁgure the Register Transfer Level (RTL) with the build conﬁguration options
•
How to integrate RAM arrays
•
How to run test patterns
•
The processes to sign oﬀ on the conﬁgured design
The Arm product deliverables include reference scripts and information about using them to
implement your design. Reference methodology ﬂows supplied by Arm are example reference
implementations. Contact your EDA vendor for EDA tool support.

About CMN S3(AE)
CMN S3(AE) is conﬁgured using the Arm®Socrates™ IP Tooling platform. The
documentation for the Arm®Socrates™ IP Tooling platform can only be found
in the Arm®Socrates™ product download bundle and includes the following
documentation:
User Guide
The Arm®Socrates™User Guide describes how to use the Arm®Socrates™
IP Tooling platform to conﬁgure and integrate a custom mesh interconnect.
Conﬁgurable options include size and device placement and an optional
System Level Cache (SLC). For more information on conﬁguring the
Arm®Socrates™ IP Tooling platform, see the Arm® Socrates™ User Guide.
Installation Guide
The Arm®Socrates™ Installation Guide describes how to install Arm®Socrates™
IP Tooling platform. For more information on installing the Arm®Socrates™ IP
Tooling platform, see the Arm® Socrates™ Installation Guide.
Design ﬂow
CMN S3(AE) is delivered as synthesizable RTL. Before it can be used in a product, it must go
through the following processes:
Implementation
The implementer conﬁgures and synthesizes the RTL to produce a hard macrocell. This
process includes integrating RAMs into the design.
Integration
The integrator connects the implemented design into an SoC. This process includes
connecting a memory system and peripherals.
Programming
Programming is the last process. The system programmer develops the software that
is required to conﬁgure and initialize the CMN S3(AE) product, and tests the required
application software.
Each process can:
•
Be performed by a diﬀerent party
•
Include implementation and integration choices that aﬀect the behavior and features of the
CMN S3(AE) product
The operation of the ﬁnal device depends on:
Build conﬁguration
The implementer chooses the options that aﬀect how the RTL source ﬁles are pre-processed.
These options usually include or exclude logic that aﬀects one or more of the area, maximum
frequency, and features of the resulting macrocell.

Conﬁguration inputs
The integrator conﬁgures some features of the CMN S3(AE) product by tying inputs to
speciﬁc values. These conﬁgurations aﬀect the start-up behavior before any software
conﬁguration is made. They can also limit the options available to the software.
Software conﬁguration
The programmer conﬁgures the CMN S3(AE) product by programming particular values into
registers. The register conﬁguration aﬀects the behavior of the CMN S3(AE) product.
This book refers to IMPLEMENTATION DEFINED features that are applicable to build
conﬁguration options. A reference to a feature that is included means that the
appropriate build and pin conﬁguration options are selected. A reference to an
enabled feature means a feature that the software has conﬁgured.

Functional description
2. Functional description
This chapter describes the functionality that is achieved when you design and conﬁgure the CMN
S3(AE) interconnect and its components.
2.1 Components and structural conﬁguration
When conﬁguring CMN S3(AE), the components you select depend on the required functionality.
The selected components, topology, and other conﬁgurable options aﬀect the overall structure of
CMN S3(AE) and the associated behavior.
This section contains the following subsections:
•
Components describes the individual interconnect components that form CMN S3(AE).
•
System conﬁgurations describes the possible system-level interconnect topologies, including
example interconnect conﬁgurations.
•
CML system conﬁgurations describes the possible CML system topologies, including example
conﬁgurations and information about speciﬁc CML options.
•
Structural conﬁguration and considerations describes optional conﬁgurations that impact the
structure and behavior of CMN S3(AE).
2.1.1 Components
CMN S3(AE) is made up of various types of devices, including router modules, CHI nodes, and
bridges. The components that you require depend on the requirements of your system and some
are optional or only used if certain requirements are met.
CMN S3(AE) can be integrated into a complete SoC system that includes devices that are not
described in this section.
2.1.1.1 Crosspoint
The crosspoint (XP) is a switch or router logic module. It is the fundamental component building
block of the CMN S3(AE) transport mechanism.
The terms XP and Mesh Crosspoint (MXP or SMXP) are used interchangeably
throughout this TRM
The CMN S3(AE) mesh interconnect is built using a set of XP modules. The XP modules are
arranged in a two-dimensional rectangular mesh topology. Each XP can connect to up to four

conﬁgurations.

2.1.1.2 I/O coherent Request Node
The I/O-coherent Request Node (RN-I) connects I/O-coherent AMBA® Requesters to the rest of
the CMN S3(AE) system.
An RN-I bridge includes up to three ACE-Lite or ACE-Lite-with-DVM completer ports, with AR,
AW, W, R, and B channels. An RN-D bridge includes up to three ACI-Lite-with-DVM completer
ports, with AR, AW, W, R, B, AC, and CR channels.
The RN-I bridge can act as a proxy only for requesters that do not contain hardware-coherent
caches. There is no capability to issue snoop transactions to RN-Is.
The DVM Request Node (RN-D) is a version of the RN-I bridge that includes DVM support
2.1.1.3 Fully coherent Home Node
The Fully coherent Home Node (HN-F) is responsible for managing part of the address space.
The HN-F consists of the following:
System Level Cache
The System Level Cache (SLC) is a last-level cache. The SLC allocation policy is exclusive for
data lines, except where sharing patterns are detected and pseudo-inclusive for code lines,
as indicated by the RN-Fs. All code lines can be allocated into the SLC on the initial request.
When MTE is enabled, SLC stores data and tags.
Combined PoS/PoC
The combined Point-of-Serialization/Point-of-Coherency (PoS/PoC) is responsible for the
ordering of all memory requests sent to the HN-F. Ordering includes serialization of multiple
outstanding requests and actions to the same fragment.
Snoop Filter
The Snoop Filter (SF) tracks cachelines that are present in the RN-Fs. It reduces snoop
traﬃc in the system by favoring directed snoops over snoop broadcasts when possible. This
approach substantially reduces the snoop response traﬃc that might otherwise be required.
Each HN-F in the system is conﬁgured to manage a speciﬁc portion of the overall address space.
The speciﬁc portion of address space will be dictated by the SAM mappings asoutlined in RN SAM
and HN-F SAM programming.
The entire DRAM space is managed through the combination of all HN-Fs in the system.
The HN-F is architecturally deﬁned to manage only well-behaved memory. Well-
behaved memory refers to memory without any possible side eﬀects. The HN-F
includes micro-architectural optimizations to exploit this architectural guarantee.
Copyright © 2023–2025 Arm Limited (or its aﬃliates). All rights reserved.

2.1.1.4 Super Home Node
The Super Home Node (HN-S) is responsible for managing part of the local address space and
managing local coherency for part of the remote address space.
The HN-S has dual functionality acting as an HN-F for local coherent memory and LCN for remote
coherent memory and hence is typically used in multi-chip conﬁgurations. HN-S allows caching
of remote addresses which allows local sharing without going oﬀ-chip. Local memory bound
transactions targeting HN-F are referred as Home Bound Transactions (HBT) and remote memory
bound transactions targeting LCN for local coherency resolution are referred as LCN Bound
transactions (LBT).
In this book any descriptions related to the HN-F also apply to the HN-S.
The HN-S consists of the following:
System Level Cache
The System Level Cache (SLC) is shared between HBT and LBT lines.
Part of the SLC used for LBT lines is referred as Local Coherent Cache (LCC).
The SLC is a last-level cache for HBT lines. The SLC allocation policy is exclusive for data lines,
except where sharing patterns are detected and pseudo-inclusive for code lines, as indicated by
the RN Fs. All code lines can be allocated into the SLC on the initial request. When MTE is enabled,
SLC stores data and tags.
For more information about how to partition SLC between HBT and LBT lines, see HN-S SLC and
LCC capacity partitioning.
Combined PoS/PoC
The combined Point-of-Serialization (PoS) and Point-of-Coherency (PoC) is responsible
for the ordering of all memory and snoop requests sent to the HN-S. Ordering includes
serialization of multiple outstanding requests/snoops and actions to the same line fragment.
Snoop Filter
The Snoop Filter (SF) tracks cachelines that are present in the RN-Fs. It reduces snoop
traﬃc in the system by favoring directed snoops over snoop broadcasts when possible. This
approach substantially reduces the snoop response traﬃc that might otherwise be required.
SF is shared between HBT and LBT lines.
Copyright © 2023–2025 Arm Limited (or its aﬃliates). All rights reserved.
Non-Conﬁdential

® Neoverse™ CMN S3(AE) Coherent Mesh Network

Functional description
Each HN-S in the system is conﬁgured to manage a speciﬁc portion of the overall local address
space and remote address space. The entire DRAM space is managed through the combination of
all HN-Ss in the system.
The HN-S is architecturally deﬁned to manage only well-behaved memory. Well-
behaved memory refers to memory without any possible side eﬀects. The HN-S
includes microarchitectural optimizations to exploit this architectural guarantee.
2.1.1.5 I/O Home Node
The I/O Home Node (HN-I) is a Home Node for all CHI transactions targeting AMBA® Completer
devices.
The HN-I acts as a proxy for all the RNs of CMN S3(AE), converting CHI transactions to ACE5-Lite
transactions. The HN-I includes support for the correct ordering of Arm device types.
The HN-I does not support caching of any data read from or written to the downstream ACE5-
Lite I/O Completer subsystem. Any cacheable or coherent request that is sent to the HN-I does
not result in any snoops being sent to RN-Fs in the system. Instead, the request is converted to the
appropriate ACE5-Lite read or write command and sent to the downstream ACE5-Lite subsystem.
If an RN-F caches data that is read from or written to the downstream ACE5-Lite
I/O Completer subsystem, coherency is not maintained. Any subsequent access to
that data reads from or writes to the ACE5-Lite I/O Completer subsystem directly,
ignoring the cached data.
2.1.1.6 I/O Home Node with PCIe peer-to-peer optimization
The I/O Home Node with PCIe peer-to-peer optimization (HN-P) is a device that includes the HN-I
functionality and dedicated trackers for PCIe peer-to-peer traﬃc.
HN-P can only be used to connect to PCIe Completers.
2.1.1.7 SBSX
The AMBA® CHI to ACE5-Lite bridge (SBSX) functions as a CHI SN-F and enables an ACE5-Lite
Completer device to be used in a CMN S3(AE) system.

2.1.1.8 Memory Tag Subordinate Interface
The Memory Tag Subordinate Interface (MTSX) node connects AXI subordinate devices without
memory tagging support to a CHI-E interconnect that requires MTE support.
MTSX contains two internal elements, an SBSX element and a Memory Tag Unit (MTU) element.
The MTU element is made up of the following parts:
•
Tag Control Queue (TCQ)
•
Optional Tag Cache (TC)
In the HN-F SAM, MTSX can only be targeted using non-hashed SN target-based SAM
programming.
2.1.1.9 CML
A Coherent Multichip Link (CML) device enables multi-chip communication in CMN S3(AE).
A given multi-chip link can be used for:
•
SMP (CML_SMP) connection can be conﬁgured for 64B or 256B ﬂit formats that support a
PCIe PHY/controller
•
CXL device attachment
•
CHI Chip-to-Chip (C2C) IO coherent attachment
A CML device (CCG) can be conﬁgured to be used for CHI C2C, CML_SMP connection or CXL
device attachment. A CXSDB will be required to interface to a 1024 bit CXS interface.
For CML_SMP connection an I/O coherent Requesting Node (RN-I) must be included in the CCG
block to support PCIe traﬃc targeting remote addresses.
CML port-to-port forwarding
CMN S3(AE) supports multiple CML gateway (CCG) blocks, each with its own CXS connection.
For CXS connections conﬁgured for CML_SMP protocol, CMN S3(AE) can pass CML_SMP traﬃc
from one CXS connection to another through the mesh, eliminating the requirement for external
switching logic.
The CCG allows for multiple topologies to be built because of the following capabilities:
•
Communicating with up to three remote CCGs
•
Port-to-port forwarding
The port-to-port forwarding feature allows the CMN S3(AE) mesh to act as a switch between
two CML_SMP chips, allowing various multi-chip topologies where the chips are not physically
connected. Each CCG can communicate with up to three remote CCGs through the same physical
connection, CXS, allowing up to two hops on a given CML_SMP network.

2.1.1.10 Conﬁguration node
The conﬁguration node (CFG) is co-located with the HN-D node and handles various CMN S3(AE)
conﬁguration, control, and monitoring features.
The CFG carries out the following functions:
•
Conﬁguration accesses
•
Error reporting and signaling
•
Interrupt generation
The CFG includes the following elements:
•
Ports to collect error signals from CHI components within CMN S3(AE)
•
A conﬁguration bus which connects to all nodes to handle internal conﬁguration register reads
and writes
•
A dedicated APB interface for conﬁguration accesses
The CFG does not have a dedicated CHI port. It shares a device port with the HN-D node in the
mesh.
2.1.1.11 Power/Clock Control Block
The Power/Clock Control Block (PCCB), co-located with the HN-D node, provides separate
communication channels. These channels pass information about the power and clock management
between the SoC and the network.
The PCCB acts as an aggregator to convey information between the SoC and the other CMN
S3(AE) components, in the following manner:
1.
The PCCB receives transaction activity indicators from other relevant CMN S3(AE) components
and conveys that information to the external power and clock control units.
2.
The PCCB receives power or clock control management requests from the external power
or clock control units. Where applicable, it conveys that request to the relevant CMN S3(AE)
components.
3.
The PCCB waits for the appropriate responses from the relevant CMN S3(AE) components, and
conveys an aggregated response to the external power and clock control units.
Copyright © 2023–2025 Arm Limited (or its aﬃliates). All rights reserved.

The PCCB does not have a dedicated CHI port. It shares a device port with the HN-D node in the

If you conﬁgure CMN S3(AE) to have multiple asynchronous clock domains, then the PCCB drives
one clock signal to each clock domain. For more information about asynchronous clock domain
support, see Clock domain conﬁgurations.
2.1.1.12 System Address Map
Every requester that is connected to CMN S3(AE) has the same view of memory.
The entire addressable space can be partitioned into subregions, and each partition must be
designated as one of the following:
I/O space
HN-I, HN-D, HN-P, HN-T, and HN-V service requests to I/O space.
DDR space
HN-F, SN-F, SBSX, and MTSX service requests to DDR space.
Unmapped addresses are routed to the HN-D.
Each HN-F covers a mutually exclusive portion of the system address space. The options and
constraints for HN-Fs are:
•
Each HN-F can contain an SLC
•
HN-Fs can be combined into System Cache Groups (SCGs)
•
Each HN-F in an SCG must have the same SLC partition size
•
An address hash function determines the target HN-F within an SCG
All CHI transactions require a target ID to route packets from source to destination. For
addressable requests, a System Address Map (SAM) determines the target ID. Each node that can
generate a CHI addressable request contains a SAM:
RN SAM
Present for all RNs and CCG HA nodes. Generates a target ID for requests to HN-F, HN-I,
HN-D, HN-P, HN-T, HN-V, SBSX, MTSX, SN-F, and CCG nodes.
HN-F SAM
Present in all HN-Fs. Generates a target ID for requests to SN-F, SBSX, MTSX, and CCG (for
CXL.mem Type3) nodes.
HN-I SAM
Present in all HN-Is. Maps the address of the incoming CHI request to an I/O subregion for
ordering purposes.

2.1.1.13 Debug and Trace Controller
The Debug and Trace Controller (DTC) controls distributed Debug and Trace Monitors (DTM) and
generates time stamped trace using the ATB interface.
The DTC performs the following functions:
•
Generates event or PMU-based interrupts
•
Receives packets from DTM and packs them into ATB format trace
•
Time stamps trace with SoC timer input
•
Generates alignment sync for the ATB trace output
•
Handles ATB ﬂush requests
•
Handles debug and Secure debug external requests
•
Provides a consistent view of distributed and central PMU counters
•
Handles PMU snapshot requests
•
Generates interrupt INTREQPMU assertion on overﬂow of PMU counters
2.1.1.14 QoS regulator
CMN S3(AE) supports end-to-end Quality-of-Service (QoS) which guarantees using QoS
mechanisms that are distributed throughout the system.
The QoS provision uses the QoS ﬁeld in each RN request packet to inﬂuence arbitration priority at
every QoS decision point. The QoS ﬁeld is then propagated through all secondary packets issued
by a request packet. RNs must either:
•
Self-modulate their QoS priority depending on how well their respective QoS requirements are
met
•
Use the integrated QoS regulators at ingress points to CMN S3(AE)
It is possible to include non-QoS-aware devices in the system, but still have these devices meet
the QoS modulation requirement of the QoS architecture. To meet this requirement, CMN S3(AE)
includes inline regulators that perform the QoS functionality without the requesting device
requiring any awareness of QoS. A QoS Regulator (QR) provides an interstitial layer between an RN
and the interconnect. The QR monitors how the bandwidth and latency requirements of the RN
are met, and does in-line replacement of the RN-provided QoS ﬁeld. The QR adjusts the QoS ﬁeld
upwards for higher priority in the system and downwards for lower priority.

2.1.1.16 Credited Slices
You can conﬁgure various optional credited register slices in your CMN S3(AE) system. These
Credited Slices can help with timing closure.
Credited Slices enable synchronous but higher latency communication at any point in the system.
CMN S3(AE) includes the following optional Credited Slices:
Mesh Credited Slice
Placed between XPs. See Mesh Credited Slice.
Asynchronous Mesh Credited Slice
Placed between XPs that are in diﬀerent clock domains. For more information, see
Asynchronous Mesh Credited Slice.
Device Credited Slice
Placed between a device and a CAL, or a device and an XP. For more information, see Device
Credited Slice.
CAL Credited Slice
Placed between a CAL and an XP. See CAL Credited Slice.
HCAL Credited Slice
Placed between an HCAL and an XP. See CAL Credited Slice.
The slices are simple repeater-ﬂop structures that are applied across the entire communication
boundary. The supported number of Credited Slices of each type is speciﬁes the supported number
in Device placement and conﬁguration.

example mesh includes two MCSs, a DCS, and a CCS.

2.1.1.17 Mesh Credited Slice
You can conﬁgure one or more Mesh Credited Slices (MCSs) between CMN S3(AE) XPs. MCSs are
optional register slices that can help timing closure in a CMN S3(AE) system.
The CMN S3(AE) mesh can operate with a single cycle of latency between XPs. However,
depending on the fabrication process and the distance between XPs, a single-cycle XP-XP
connection might limit frequency. In this case, one or more MCSs can be added to lengthen
the XP-XP links. Register slices add link transfer latency, but also allow certain CMN S3(AE)
implementations to run at higher frequencies.
Each MCS on an XP-XP link adds an extra cycle between XPs. One to four MCSs can be added to
any link between XPs.
Copyright © 2023–2025 Arm Limited (or its aﬃliates). All rights reserved.
Non-Conﬁdential

@@@PAGE 69@@@

® Neoverse™ CMN S3(AE) Coherent Mesh Network
Technical Reference Manual
Document ID: 107858_0203_05_en
Issue 05
Functional description
A conﬁgurable buﬀer depth of 2-4 is allowed and you can select it using the
MCS_RXBUF_NUM_ENTRIES parameter.
For timing, you can enable an optional register slice on the PUB, internal communications system,
interface using the MCS_PUB_RSL_EN parameter. By default, register slices are only applied to the
CHI interfaces.
2.1.1.18 Asynchronous Mesh Credited Slice
CMN S3(AE) supports multiple asynchronous clock domains across the mesh. Asynchronous Mesh
Credited Slices (AMCSs) perform clock domain crossing between two asynchronous mesh clock
domains.
To conﬁgure multiple clock domains in the mesh, you must also conﬁgure an AMCS on all XP-XP
links that span diﬀerent clock domains. Up to four MCS can be included along with AMCs in any
sequence on the XP-XP link.
The AMCS does not perform frequency scaling, it only synchronizes traﬃc between
asynchronous clock domains. All CMN S3(AE) clock domains must operate at the
same frequency.
When using AMCSs to create multiple asynchronous clock domains, you must divide the mesh into
four quadrants, each with a single clock domain. These quadrants must be rectangular and include
one or more XPs.
For more information about CMN S3(AE) support for asynchronous clock domains, see Clock
domain conﬁgurations.
The following ﬁgure shows an example CMN S3(AE) topology with four asynchronous clock
domains that AMCSs bridge. The clock domains must be arranged in the order that the following
ﬁgure shows. Clock domain 0 must be the bottom-left quadrant.

2.1.3.1 CML Symmetric Multiprocessor (SMP) support
A Symmetric Multiprocessor (SMP) allows for a shared, common OS and memory to operate on
multiple chips.
CMN S3(AE) supports SMP systems when the systems are built using the same version of CMN
S3(AE). For SMP systems, CCG block is required to enable multi-chip SMP communications over a
CXS issue B interface.
When set, the provided SMP mode option enables DVM, GIC-D, Exclusives, MPAM, CPU-Event,
and selective CHI-D, CHI-E, CHI-F and CHI-G features across CML_SMP links using a micro-
architected mechanism.
Trace Tag, when set on CHI request or snoop, is preserved across CML_SMP link.
For more information about programming CMN S3(AE) for SMP mode, see CML programming.
2.1.3.1.1
CML Hybrid SMP Fully Coherent Accelerator support
CMN S3(AE) has the capability to be conﬁgured in a CML_SMP system where the connected chips
have asymmetrical conﬁgurations and devices. When conﬁgured in this way, it can function as a
fully coherent accelerator.

To enable CPAG, both RN SAM and HN-F registers must be programmed accordingly in each chip.
2.1.3.3 CML credit requirements
Each CML port requires a minimum of one request and one data credit more than the total number
of reservations. This number is enabled through the conﬁguration control register of the RA
(por_ccg_ra_cfg_ctl).
This requirement applies to each enabled CML_SMP link end at a given CML port. For example, by
default all the reservations are enabled in the SMP mode. Therefore, a minimum of four request
and four data credits must be granted per CML link end. These credits are used by certain traﬃc
types, such as QoS-15 or PCIe, to progress in a loaded system. See por_ccg_ra_cfg_ctl.
2.1.3.4 Tunneling PCIe traﬃc through CML_SMP link
CMN S3(AE) supports tunneling of PCIe traﬃc targeting remote memory through an CML_SMP.
Tunneling of PCIe traﬃc is advantageous if the local and remote memory is high ordered
interleaved, for example NUMA. An address range is considered to be high order interleaved
if the address range programmed in a RN SAMs hashed or non-hashed address region is either
targeting remote memory or local memory but not both. An address range is considered low
ordered interleaved if the programmed address range is striped across both local and remote HNs.
Usually low order interleaving using RN SAMs same address region is only expected for HN-F
bound memory. Tunneling requires a sigular path from the requester to the target. If the address
range is considered low order interleaved, the tunnel cannot be maintained as the requester has to
change its target when it crosses the address interleaving boundary.
To enable this function, the CCG on the remote chip must contain an RN-I. You achieve this by
using one of the CCG*PCI* node types. You must program local PCIe RN-I, RN-D, and CCG blocks
accordingly to enable this traﬃc. A PCIe RN-I or RN-D has PCIe IP connected to an ACE-Lite
interface, and has the pcie_mstr_present conﬁguration register bit set.
2.1.3.5 PCIe writes
To optimize PCIe write bandwidth targeting remote memory the originating PCIe RN-I or RN-D
must use AXID based hashing to the CCG. A PCIe RN-I or RN-D sends these writes to CCG in
pipe-lined fashion.
The CCG also issues early completion for intermediate (non-last) data beats for write burst
requests originating from the same AXI burst sent to the PCIe RN-I or RN-D. This behavior helps
to reduce tracker lifetime and increases the number of outstanding requests from the PCIe RN-I or
RN-D.
If these writes are targeting a remote PCIe EP through HN-P, then CCG also preserves additional
information across SMP link. This behavior helps with gathering of these writes downstream of
remote HN-P. To enable write gathering at the endpoint, the CCG creates uniquely identiﬁable
Copyright © 2023–2025 Arm Limited (or its aﬃliates). All rights reserved.

write streams coming from diﬀerent RN-Is and RN-Ds in the system. To create unique streams, the
CCG sends the following information to the remote CCG RN-I:
•
The Chip ID
•
Logical RN-I/D (RAID)
•

Remote CCG RN-I then issues a request to HN-P with all the identifying information that can be
used downstream of HN-P to gather write bursts.
For more information about RN-I and RN-D write burst cracking and write gathering ﬂow, see RN-I
and RN-D write Burst cracking.
If an RN-I is not present at remote CCG, then write tunneling must be disabled. By default, write
tunneling is enabled.
Write tunneling in CCG can be disabled by setting the dis_rnid_tnl_retry_trk and
dis_rnid_early_wrcomp bits, and clearing the remote_rni_present bit in the por_ccg_ra_aux_ctl
register.
Write tunneling at PCIe RN-I and RN-D can be disabled by setting the
dis_pci_cxra_logical_tgt_2hop bit in the por_rni_aux_ctl register.
To uniquely identify the originating PCIe RN-I and RN-D for write gathering, a unique RAID must
be assigned to each PCIe RN-I and RN-D. These RAIDs are required to be unique only across PCIe
RN-I and RN-D. There is also a software controlled CHIPID that is used to uniquely identify the
PCIe RN-I and RN-D.
If the target is remote HN-P, address-based CML Port Aggregation (CPAG) must be disabled to
preserve write ordering.
2.1.3.6 PCIe reads
Read bursts coming from PCIe RN-I and RN-D targeting PCI_CXRA node types are preserved
across CML_SMP link.
If the remote target is an HN-P, the remote CCG RN-I then further issues a read burst to HN-P. If
the remote target is an HN-F, the remote CCG RN-I cracks the read bursts into 64B chunks.
If an RN-I is not present on the remote side, that is at remote CCG, PCIe Read
bursts cannot be issued to a CCG.
To indicate that a remote CCG RN-I is present, set the remote_rni_present ﬁeld of
the por_ccg_ra_aux_ctl register.

2.1.3.7 Streaming PCIe write traﬃc through CML_SMP link
CMN S3(AE) supports streaming of PCIe ordered writes when targeting remote memory through
an CML_SMP.
Use this mechanism when the address range targeted by PCIe traﬃc, programmed in a given RN
SAM address region, is striped across local and remote HNs at certain interleaving granularity.
In CMN S3(AE), the interleaving granularity, below which RN-I and RN-D will use this streaming
mechanism, is set to 4K. Additionally, this mechanism can be used if PCIe write traﬃc cannot be
tunneled through a given CCG. For information about when tunneling is disabled, see Tunneling
PCIe traﬃc through CML_SMP link
For programming requirements to enable PCIe write traﬃc, see Programming to enable PCIe write
streaming through CML_SMP link.
2.1.3.8 Host side data encryption for CXL Type-3 HDM-H memory device
CMN S3(AE) supports host side data encryption MPE for data stored on a CXL Type3 HDM-H
device.
Host side MPE is expected to be enabled when a CXL switch and/or CXL device are not part of
Host’s Trusted Compute Base (TCB). The MPE block is external to CMN S3(AE), and CCG RA
conﬁgured for Type3 HDM-H communication talks to the MPE block using MPE CXS interfaces.
For more information on this MPE CXS interface, see MPE CXS Interface. For more information on
MPE functionality, refer to Memory Protection Engine Implementation and Integration Guide revision
1.0.
Memory Protection Engine Implementation and Integration Guide revision 1.0 is only
available on request.
The following attributes of the incoming request are used by the MPE to encrypt or decrypt the
data.
1.
Physical Address[51:6]
2.
PAS[1:0] = {NSE,NS}
3.
MECID [11:0]

Functional description
This version of CMN S3(AE) supports 12-bit MECID for Host side MPE.
For a read request sent to a CXL Type3 HDM-H device, CCG RA simultaneously sends the
corresponding tweak information to the MPE block. This tweak information includes Physical
Address (PA), PAS and MECID information. Sending the tweak information simultaneously helps to
hide the tweak generation latency in the MPE block. Received data response is sent to the MPE
block to be decrypted, and the decrypted data is sent to the corresponding HN-F or RN.
For a write request sent to a CXL Type3 HDM-H device, CCG RA sends the tweak information to
the MPE block at the same time when it issues a CHI DBID response to pull the data. When the
data is received from the CHI side, it is sent to the MPE block to get it encrypted.
The following are constraints when the MPE is enabled:
1.
Host side MPE can be enabled only if the CXL Type3 HDM-H device supports 64B read data
transfers (DRS)
2.
12-bits of MECID is supported
3.
CCG RA must be conﬁgured in CML_SMP Subordinate Agent (CXSA) mode
A CCG RA with MPE enabled can be conﬁgured using por_ccg_ra_cfg_ctl to ﬁlter out incoming
traﬃc for encryption based on the following conﬁgurations:
1.
ccg_ra_cfg_ctrl.mpe_non_secure_bypass_disable: When clear, non-secure data bypasses the
MPE. When set, all data, including non-secure, is sent to the MPE. This register bit polarity
allows non-secure data to be bypassed by default.
2.
ccg_ra_cfg_ctrl.mpe_mecid_ﬁlter_enable : valid bit to enable mecid based ﬁltering. If set to 0b1,
incoming request with MECID[11:0] value equal to that programmed in ccg_ra_cfgaux_ctrl.
mpe_mecid_ﬁlter bypasses the MPE.
To enable MPE feature, UDP cache line state is not supported in CMN.
To enable MPE feature in CCG RA that is connected to Type3 CXL Device,
ccg_ra_cfg_ctrl_grp.mpe_enable must be set to 0b1.
When programming CCG RA in HN-F SAM in HN-S or HN-F,
cmn_hns_sam_ccg_sa_attr.ccg_sa*_full_data_wr_en must be set to 0b1.

2.1.3.9 CCG Duplicated
CMN S3(AE) provides a CCG variant called CCG Duplicated (CCGD) for use cases where hardware
fault detection is critical.
To maximize the detection of hardware failures, the logic inside the CCG is duplicated and run
in lockstep. This allows the outputs to be compared to ensure faults are detected. The following
ﬁgure shows the block diagram describing the CCGD internals.
Figure 2-23: Duplicated CCG Block Diagram
All multi-chip gateways must be the same variant. If one gateway is a CCGD variant,
then all gateways must be CCGD variants.
The CCGD contains two instances of the CCG, and all outputs are fed synchronously into the
CCG output checker. A mismatch in this output checker raises an interrupt on the CCG_ERR_NID<x>
output that can be cleared with a reset of the CMN S3(AE).

2.1.4 Structural conﬁguration and considerations
CMN S3(AE) supports various options that you can use to further conﬁgure the structure of the
interconnect. Some of these options have speciﬁc restrictions and requirements, and modify the
behavior of the interconnect from the default behavior.
CMN S3(AE) supports the following structural options:
•
Dual DAT, REQ, RSP, and SNP channels
•
Dual RSP channels on the upload port of the CCG, CCGD, and HN-P devices
•
Dedicated RN-I resource for traﬃc through AXI ports
•
CML Port Aggregation Groups (CPAGs)
•
Using extra device ports on MXPs
•
Connection of devices with multiple interfaces
2.1.4.1 Dual CHI channels
To reduce congestion within the mesh, CMN S3(AE) provides a conﬁguration option to double the
number of CHI channels. This feature is useful when there are heavy traﬃc sources that saturate
speciﬁc routing paths.
If the EN_2X_[DAT/RSP]_VC parameter is enabled, the number of DAT and RSP CHI channels per
MXP-MXP connection increases from one to two. Each channel can be controlled independently.
This option has the following beneﬁts:
•
Increases device upload bandwidth
•
Increases MXP-MXP bandwidth
The EN_2X_REQ_VC and EN_2X_SNP_VC parameters, when enabled, add an additional pair of REQ and
SNP CHI channels.

(upload)
DAT / RSP channel 
(download)
Each mesh target is associated with one of the two DAT channels. All traﬃc to a single target is
mapped to one of the two DAT channels. Likewise, all responses and snoops are mapped to one of
the two RSP or SNP channels respectively.
The REQ channel diﬀers from the other CHI channels because it uses the SourceID to route to one
of the two REQ channels. This is done because RN-F device types that send requests into the MXP
can have their TargetID overridden when an address lookup is performed. This change in channel
selection behavior also allows for traﬃc to a single target to be received from both REQ channels.
When you enable this feature by setting the conﬁguration parameter, CMN S3(AE) applies a default
channel selection scheme. Traﬃc to targets on MXPs with an even XID uses channel 0 and traﬃc
to targets on MXPs with an odd XID uses channel 1. This scheme is active until you specify a new
scheme at boot by programming the channel selection behavior. See Program the dual channel
selection scheme.
The MESH_2X_DEF_SEL parameter value aﬀects the default selection scheme in the following way:

channels are not aﬀected.

a single mesh channel and no route decode logic is needed within the SMXP for RSP ﬂits received
from the device.
2.1.4.3 Dual CHI channel selection registers
Boot-programmable registers deﬁne the TargetID-based LUT. The MXP uses this LUT to select CHI
channels for ﬂits on the DAT, RSP, and SNP channels. The REQ channel only uses SourceID XID or
YID based routing.
If the dual CHI channel feature is enabled, using por_mxp_multi_mesh_chn_sel_*, then each MXP
contains 16 64-bit registers. The contents of these registers deﬁne the LUT that selects which
channel a ﬂit is assigned to. Each register can specify the assignment channel for four TargetIDs, so
you can conﬁgure the behavior for up to 64 targets overall.
After the dual CHI registers have been programmed, any remaining unprogrammed TargetIDs are
automatically assigned to channel 0. Unprogrammed registers and ﬁelds hold the reset value and
are not part of the lookup. Programmed registers and ﬁelds are only valid for lookup when the
multi_mesh_chn_sel_reg_*_valid bit of the register is set.
The following table shows the register format. Each 11-bit TargetID + CHN_SEL ﬁeld speciﬁes a
TargetID and the CHI channel for ﬂits with that TargetID.

2.1.4.4 Dedicated RN-I resources for AXI port traﬃc
You can set up dedicated resources per AXI port in the RN-I and RN-D. Using this feature, you can
ensure that one requester that is connected to an RN-I or RN-D does not block progress of traﬃc
from another requester.
For example, you can use this feature to connect SMMU and GIC components to RN-I or RN-D
AXI ports, and ensure that real-time traﬃc from both components can progress.
To support this feature, the RN-I and RN-D have two sets of conﬁguration registers per port and an
auxiliary control register. You must program these registers to enable this feature.
Programming the registers for a port reserves a speciﬁc number of tokens for that port. When
these tokens are reserved, the requester that is attached to that port is guaranteed an equivalent
number of tracker entries and corresponding resources. Other requesters that are connected to
the RN-I or RN-D are blocked from using these reserved resources. Therefore, traﬃc from the
requester with reserved tokens can progress. You can divide up RN-I or RN-D resources between
diﬀerent ports according to the relative resource requirements of diﬀerent requesters.
The following table shows the conﬁguration registers that you program to enable this feature. The
table also shows the associated register ﬁelds and some properties of those ﬁelds.
Table 2-8: Conﬁguration register ﬁelds for dedicated GIC and MMU RN-I resources
Register name
Register ﬁeld
Bits
Reset
value
Description

reservation.

For each port, software can program the number of tokens that correspond to the number of
reserved entries in the tracker per slice. The token ﬁelds are 7 bits wide to accommodate the
maximum tracker size of 128 entries. For a smaller tracker size, only the appropriate bit ranges are
used. For example, for a 16-entry tracker, only bits [3:0] of the 7-bit ﬁeld are used to indicate the
number of reserved tokens.
When you enable this feature using the dis_port_token ﬁeld of the por_rni_cfg_ctl register, QoS15-
based reservation is disabled.

If s0_rd_token = 0
One tracker entry is reserved, if the total number of the programmed reserved entries from
all ports is larger than the number of read tracker entries in the slice minus 1, the number
of tokens has been misprogrammed. To prevent overﬂow because of misprogramming, the
RN-I reserves a speciﬁc number of tokens for each port. The RN-I uses a quarter of the
programmed value of each port to calculate the number of reserved entries. If this value is a
fraction, then the remainder is rounded to 0.
Programmed values for eight-entry tracker
Consider the following programmed values for a tracker with eight entries:
s0_port_token = 4
Reserving ﬁve entries
s1_port_token = 0
Reserving one entry
s2_port_token = 1
Reserving two entries
In this case, the total number of reserved entries is eight, and the tracker has no unreserved
entries. However, the number of tracker entries minus one is seven, and so the registers are
misprogrammed. In this case, the RN-I divides each register value by four to calculate the ﬁnal
number of reserved entries.
s0 = 4/4 = 1
Two entries are reserved
s1 = 0/4 = 0
One entry is reserved
s2 = 1/2 = 0
One entry is reserved
Therefore, a total of four entries are reserved for this conﬁguration. The tracker has four
unreserved entries.
2.1.4.5 Support for extra device ports on MXPs

activity between MXPs.
The maximum permitted number of device ports per MXP is conﬁguration-dependent.
Enabling extra device ports aﬀects the following aspects of CMN S3(AE):

The overall system topology. See Topology considerations when using extra device ports.

2.1.4.7 DTM changes when using extra device ports
A conﬁguration parameter determines whether DTMs are replicated in MXPs to support extra
device ports. Each port is mapped to a speciﬁc DTM and both the conﬁguration parameter value
and the overall system conﬁguration determines how the ports are mapped.
For a mesh conﬁguration, up to four device ports are permitted per MXP. For more
information, see Topology considerations when using extra device ports.
To enable support for multiple DTMs in MXPs, set the MXP_MULTIPLE_DTM_EN parameter = 1. If
this parameter is set to 1, then the DTM in each MXP is replicated according to the number of
device ports on the MXP. Each DTM supports up to two device ports. The diﬀerent interconnect
conﬁgurations use the following DTM mappings:
Mesh conﬁguration
•
DTM0 supports P0 and P1
•
DTM1 supports P2 and P3
If the MXP_MULTIPLE_DTM_EN parameter = 0, each MXP has a single DTM. In this case, for mesh
conﬁgurations the single DTM supports P0, P1, P2, and P3.
If a single DTM supports more than two ports, it might not be possible to monitor
all the events on diﬀerent ports at the same time. However, using a single DTM
saves on the implementation area.
2.1.5 DSU, DMC and MXP AXI5 Utility Bus
CMN S3(AE) provides a mechanism to interface with an AXI5 Utility Bus (AXU), which is a
simpliﬁed version of AXI5.
The accesses can be either 32b or 64b in size, and single data transfer with no burst. The AXU is
connected to RN-F and SN-F node locations as an AXI5 requester port.
AXU is conﬁgurable for RN-F-*FSAM and SN-FF locations. It can be conﬁgured on
all MXPs. When MXPAXU is present, DSU and DMC cannot be supported.
Each AXU port has a logical ID. One set of logical IDs are contiguously numbered for
RN-F, and another set are contiguously numbered for SN-F. For MXP AXU, it is indexed
by the MXP Logical ID. To send a request to those ports, software must look up the

The DSU address region starts from DSU_PERIPHBASE. Depending on the conﬁguration, each DSU
occupies a 1MB, 4MB, 16MB, or 64MB ﬁxed space. CMN S3(AE) supports up to 1GB in total DSU
address space. You can calculate the total DSU address space, in MB, using the total number of
DSUs rounded up to next power of 2. A base aligned with this address space must be driven to
DSU_PERIPHBASE. To access the DSU, the address is composed of the lower bits, up to the maximum
address of each DSU, and the higher bits below the DSU peripheral base, to indicate the logical ID
of each DSU.
The DMC address region starts from DMC_PERIPHBASE. Depending on the conﬁguration, each DMC
occupies a 1MB, 4MB, 16MB, or 64MB ﬁxed space. CMN S3(AE) supports up to 1GB in total DMC
address space. You can calculate the total DMC address space, in MB, using the total number of
DMCs rounded up to the next power of 2. A base aligned with this address space must be driven
to DMC_PERIPHBASE. To access the DMC, the address is composed of the lower bits, up to the
maximum address of each DMC, and the higher bits below the DMC peripheral base, to indicate
the logical ID of each DMC.
The MXP AXU address region starts from MXP_AXU_PERIPHBASE. Depending on the conﬁguration,
each MXP AXU occupies a 1MB, 4MB, 16MB, or 64MB ﬁxed space. CMN S3(AE) supports up
to 1GB in total MXP AXU address space. You can calculate the total MXP AXU address space, in
MB, using the total number of MXP AXUs rounded up to next power of 2. A base aligned with
this address space must be driven to MXP_AXU_PERIPHBASE. To access the MXP AXU, the address
is composed of the lower bits, up to the maximum address of each MXP AXU, and the higher bits
below the MXP AXU peripheral base, to indicate the logical ID of each MXP AXU.
To facilitate APB access, we recommend that all four bases, CFGM_PERIPHBASE, DSU_PERIPHBASE,
DMC_PERIPHBASE, and MXP_AXU_PERIPHBASE reside in the same lower 4GB aligned space. Bits
[31:28] must be diﬀerent between CFGM_PERIPHBASE, DSU_PERIPHBASE, or DMC_PERIPHBASE, and
MXP_AXU_PERIPHBASE. Each of the four PERIPHBASE values are determined by the associated input
strap signals.
For DMC/DSU, the APB access indicator is carried on AxPROT[0]. See
por_axu_control
2.1.6 MXP Device Isolation
HN-F or HN-S devices attached to a CAL2 can be logically isolated from the corresponding MXP
and mesh.
Output signals from the HN-F or HN-S are driven to benign values in the CAL2. For example,
the valid bit outputs are driven to 0b0. This isolation occurs by default if the DEVICE_ISO_EN
conﬁguration parameter is enabled.
Copyright © 2023–2025 Arm Limited (or its aﬃliates). All rights reserved.
Non-Conﬁdential
Page 96 of 2184

@@@PAGE 97@@@
Arm
® Neoverse™ CMN S3(AE) Coherent Mesh Network
Technical Reference Manual
Document ID: 107858_0203_05_en
Issue 05
Functional description
Conﬁguration writes to the MXP por_mxp_device_port_disable registers are required to remove the
isolation after reset if the DEVICE_ISO_EN conﬁguration parameter is enabled. This needs to occur
early in the boot process since any CHI or conﬁguration transactions targeting an isolated HN-F or
HN-S will not complete and may cause hangs. In addition, the CMN P-Channel cannot transition to
the ON state since the HN-F or HN-S devices are isolated, and the RAM initialization sequences
will not complete.
The default RN SAM conﬁguration does not allow independent targetIDs for HN-F or HN-S
devices behind the CAL2, so both devices must be isolated when using the CAL2 mode in the RN
SAM. The RNSAM_NUM_ADD_HASHED_TGT parameter must be used to allow individual targetIDs for
each HN-F or HN-S device behind the CAL2, allowing isolation of the individual HN-F or HN-S
devices.
The following is an example of the post-reset sequence using the isolation feature to enable the
non-isolated HN-F or HN-S devices, and initialize the RAMs:
1.
Transition the CMN P-Channel to CONFIG state on reset de-assertion, see Power domain
control.
2.
For each non-isolated HN-F or HN-S: program corresponding MXP
por_mxp_device_port_disable registers to disable isolation of corresponding CAL2 device port.
3.
For each non-isolated HN-F or HN-S: conﬁgure the PPU registers to initialize RAMs, transition
OFF->FAM state or OFF->SFONLY state if SLC is 0KB, see HN-F power domains.
4.
Transition CMN P-Channel to ON state, see Power domain control.
5.
Conﬁgure CMN SAMs and overall system address map to avoid disabled HN-F or HN-S
devices.
The HN-F or HN-S isolation status can be determined by the discovery process, indication is in the
corresponding child_pointer[30] register.bit for each HN-F and HN-S. For more information, see
Child pointers.

Not supported from RN-I and RN-D on compute chiplet and remote specialized IOM
chiplet.
•
Port forwarding is not supported for a heterogeneous conﬁguration, which means that all the
specialized IOM chips must be fully connected to each other.
2.2 Clocks and resets
CMN S3(AE) provides a hierarchical clocking microarchitecture which enables dynamic clock
management for power eﬃciency. It also has a global reset signal.
CMN S3(AE) has a High-level Clock Gating (HCG) mechanism for clock signal management during
periods of inactivity. See High-level Clock Gating.
2.2.1 Clock domain conﬁgurations
CMN S3(AE) supports either one synchronous or multiple asynchronous clock domains.

Each asynchronous clock domain is supplied by an individual clock input. These clock signals are
known as GCLK0, GCLK1, GCLK2, and GCLK3, and collectively referred to as GCLKn.
If you conﬁgure the CMN S3(AE) mesh to use multiple asynchronous clock domains, you must
comply with the following restrictions:
•
AMCSs must bridge asynchronous clock domains. Therefore, you must place AMCSs on the XP-
XP links that span clock domains.
•
The individual clock signals that supply each clock domain must run at the same frequency as
each other, although they can be asynchronous.
•
CMN S3(AE) only supports rectangular clock domains containing one or more XPs. L-shaped or
other clock domain topologies are not supported.
•
2 x 2 and smaller mesh conﬁgurations do not support multiple clock domains.

A single Q-Channel controls all the clock signals. Therefore the clock domains cannot be gated

2.2.3 Clock hierarchy
The clocking delivery and clock gating architecture are hierarchical.
Within the clock gating hierarchy, the following levels of clocks are deﬁned:
Global clock
The global clock is the clock input to the CMN S3(AE) system. Another level of clock gating
or clock control outside of the system is likely to control the global clock that is provided by
the SoC. Although it is not a system requirement, CMN S3(AE) includes support for external
clock control.
If you conﬁgure CMN S3(AE) to use multiple asynchronous clock domains, a single
Q-Channel controls each individual clock signal. Therefore, the individual clock
domains cannot be separately gated. See Clock domain conﬁgurations.
Copyright © 2023–2025 Arm Limited (or its aﬃliates). All rights reserved.
Non-Conﬁdential
Page 104 of 2184

@@@PAGE 105@@@
Arm
® Neoverse™ CMN S3(AE) Coherent Mesh Network
Technical Reference Manual
Document ID: 107858_0203_05_en
Issue 05
Functional description
Regional clocks
Regional clocks are created as an output of regional clock gaters that include a coarse enable
for coarse-grained clock gating under idle or mostly idle conditions. Regional clock gaters
can shutdown the clock network between regional and local gaters. Therefore, this level
of hierarchy enables greater power reduction than is possible using local clock gating. The
regional clock gaters are instantiated in and controlled by the CMN S3(AE) RTL. The exact set
of regional clocks is internal to CMN S3(AE) and is not described in this book.
Local clocks
Local clocks are created according to the following hierarchy:
1.
RTL creates ﬁne grained enable signals
2.
Fine grained enable signals control local clock gaters
3.
Local clock gaters output local clock signals
Local clock signals are used to directly clock sequential elements in CMN S3(AE). The exact set of
local clocks is internal to CMN S3(AE) and is not described in this book.
The following ﬁgure shows the clocking hierarchy.

2.2.4 Clock enable inputs
CMN S3(AE) includes several clock enable inputs.
The following describes the relationship of the clock enable inputs to GCLK0.
If your conﬁguration uses multiple asynchronous clock domains, then the same
relationship applies to the individual global clock signals for each clock domain.
The clock enable input signals are:
ACLKEN_S
Present on each AMBA® Completer interface.
ACLKEN_M
Present on each AMBA® Requester interface.
ATCLKEN
Present on each debug and trace ATB interface.
All clock enables, shown here as CLKEN, have identical functionality, enabling the respective
interfaces with which they are included to run at integer fractions of GCLK0. The eﬀect is that the
clock enables run slower than GCLK0, ranging from ratios of 1:1 to 4:1. ATCLKEN is limited to 1:1,
2:1, and 4:1 integer fractions. This approach enables synchronous communication with slower SoC
logic.
CLKEN asserts one GCLK0 cycle before the rising edge of SoC-CLK. SoC control logic can change
the ratio of GCLK0 frequency to the SoC clock, SoC-CLK, frequency dynamically using CLKEN.
The following ﬁgure shows a timing example of a CLKEN ratio change. In the example, CLKEN
changes the ratio of the relevant interface frequency relative to GCLK0 from 3:1 to 1:1.

2.2.5 High-level Clock Gating
The PCCB supports a High-level Clock Gating (HCG) mechanism. This mechanism notiﬁes the SoC
when CMN S3(AE) is inactive and therefore reduces dynamic power consumption.
HCG enables an external SoC clock control unit, the External Clock Controller (ExtCC), to stop the
GCLKn clock inputs. For more information about the ExtCC, see External Clock Controller.
If your CMN S3(AE) conﬁguration has multiple asynchronous clock domains, the
ExtCC stops each individual global clock signal identically.
CMN S3(AE) includes a Q-Channel interface that enables CMN S3(AE) and the SoC to
communicate to achieve HCG functionality through the PCCB. See the AMBA® Low Power Interface
Speciﬁcation Arm® Q-channel and P-channel Interfaces.
2.2.6 External Clock Controller
The ExtCC is used to control the clock gating ﬂow.
The following ﬁgure shows an example of how the ExtCC controls the clock gating ﬂow. This
example clock gating sequence begins and ends with the Q-Channel in either of the following
states:
•
Quiescent state (Q_STOPPED), where QREQn and QACCEPTn are asserted
•
Active state (Q_RUN), where QREQn and QACCEPTn are deasserted

The requirements of the ExtCC are as follows:
•
It must supply a clock to CMN S3(AE) when the Q-Channel is in any state other than
Q_STOPPED.
•
The ExtCC can either choose to gate the clock to CMN S3(AE) when the Q-Channel is in the
Q_STOPPED state, or it can choose to run the clock at any time.
•
ExtCC is responsible for bringing the Q-Channel to Q_RUN state after reset deassertion.
•
Although this book does not describe the exact behavior of the ExtCC and its usage of QREQn
in response to QACTIVE deassertion, the design of the ExtCC is likely to include a control loop
with some hysteresis. Therefore HCG is enabled when the system is inactive for long periods,
but is not enabled for short periods of inactivity. If the clocks are stopped in response to short
periods of inactivity, performance of CMN S3(AE) can be negatively aﬀected.
•
It is the responsibility of the SoC designer to fully control the clock management Q-Channel.
If there is a requirement for a control or conﬁguration bit to completely enable or disable HCG
functionality, that register or bit must exist outside of CMN S3(AE). More speciﬁcally, CMN
S3(AE) has no internal means of disabling HCG.

CML CCG block runs at CMN S3(AE) clock domain (GCLKn). It adds Q-Channel interface for each

CLK_CXS Q-Channel
Manages the CXS link interface.

2.2.8 Reset
CMN S3(AE) has two global reset input signal - nSRESET and nPORESET.
•
nSRESET is the warm reset that will reset all registers except for RAS error record and DTM
FIFO.
•
nPORESET is the cold reset that will reset everything.
All paths from reset synchronizers are required to meet single cycle timing.
The reset signals are an active-LOW and can be asynchronously or synchronously asserted and
deasserted.
When asserted, resets must remain asserted for 90 clock cycles. Likewise, when deasserted, resets
must remain deasserted for 90 clock cycles. This requirement ensures that all internal CMN S3(AE)
components enter and exit their reset states correctly.
All CMN S3(AE) clock inputs must be active during the required 90-cycle, or larger, period of reset
assertion. The clock inputs must also remain active for at least 90 cycles following deassertion of
reset.
Warm reset must be either asserted or deasserted with Cold Reset or by itself. The following is the
warm reset sequence requirement for assertion and deassertion:
1.
Take all Q-channel to a Q-Stopped state. For a partial Q-channel, Q-Active must be 0.
2.
Stop the global clock for minimum cycles.
3.
Assert Warm Reset.
4.
Start global clock.
5.
Wait for minimum cycles.
6.
Deassert Warm Reset.
Registers see diﬀerent eﬀects on cold and warm reset which includes the:

2.3 Power management
CMN S3(AE) includes several power management capabilities, that are either externally controllable
or are assisted by the SoC.
CMN S3(AE) has the following power management capabilities:
•
Several distinct predeﬁned power states. These states include ones in which all, half, or none of
the SLC Tag and Data RAMs can be powered up, powered down, or in retention:
◦
A state in which only the HN-F SF is active
◦
A state in which the SLC RAMs and SF RAMs are inactive
Copyright © 2023–2025 Arm Limited (or its aﬃliates). All rights reserved.

These power states reduce static and dynamic power consumption.
•
Support for static retention in HN-F in which the SoC places SLC and SF RAMs in a retention
state. This capability reduces static power consumption.
•
Support for in-pipeline low-latency Data RAM retention control, in which a programmable idle
counter can be used to put the SLC RAMs in retention.
The clocking hierarchy and clock gating mechanism are described in Clocks and
resets.
2.3.1 Power domains
The power domains in CMN S3(AE) are split between the logic and RAMs within the HN-F
partitions.
The power domains are:
Logic
All logic except HN-F SLC Tag and Data RAMs and HN-F SF RAMs.
System Level Cache RAM0
SLC Tag and Data RAMs way[7:0] within HN-F partitions. The RAMs in each HN-F partition
can be independently controlled.
System Level Cache RAM1
SLC Tag and Data RAMs way[15:8] within HN-F partitions. The RAMs in each HN-F partition
can be independently controlled. The RAM1 domain for 384K, 1.5MB or 3MB SLC size
conﬁgurations includes way[11:8].
Snoop ﬁlter only mode
SF RAMs within HN-F partitions. The RAMs in each HN-F partition can be independently
controlled.

2.3.2 Power domain control
The CMN S3(AE) Logic P-Channel controls all power domains except for the RAM and CXS power

2.3.3 P-Channel on device reset
This section shows how to initialize the power state of a power domain.
Certain device power states might power down the control logic. When powering this control logic
back on, the power controller must indicate the state that the device must power up. The device
detects the required state by sampling PSTATE when nSRESET deasserts. The PSTATE inputs must
be asserted before the deassertion of reset and remain after the deassertion of nSRESET, to allow
reset propagation within CMN S3(AE). The power controller must ensure that the reset sequence is
complete before transitioning PSTATE, otherwise the device might sample an undetermined value.
The following ﬁgure shows the state initialization on reset while PREQ is deasserted. CMN S3(AE)
also supports P-Channel initialization with PREQ asserted at nSRESET deassertion.
PSTATE inputs must be static 100 cycles before deassertion of nSRESET, and also
for 100 cycles after the deassertion of nSRESET.

2.3.4 HN-F Memory retention mode
When isolating the CMN S3(AE) outputs, handshake protocols on certain interfaces must be
followed. The steps list how to enter and exit HN-F Memory retention mode.
Entering HN-F Memory retention mode
1.
Program the HN-Fs to enter the required power state.
2.
Quiesce the interconnect, and wait for QACTIVE to drop.
3.
Place CMN S3(AE) in LOGIC_OFF state through the Logic P-Channel.
4.
Isolate the CMN S3(AE) outputs. If the logic on the other side of the interface is being powered
down or reset, this step might not be required.
5.
Turn oﬀ power to CMN S3(AE).

2.3.5 HN-F power domains
The HN-F has various power states. Transitioning between diﬀerent states enables or disables
diﬀerent parts of the HN-F.
The HN-F has three classes of power states:
1.
Operational states, where logic is on and enabled RAMs are operating as normal.
2.
Functional retention states, where logic is on, and enabled RAMs are in retention.
3.
Memory Retention states, where logic is oﬀ and enabled RAMs are in retention.
Within these power states, the HN-Fs in an SCG operates in four modes:
FAM
Full Associativity Mode (FAM), where the SF and the entire SLC are enabled.
HAM
Half-Associativity Mode (HAM), where the SF is enabled but the upper half of the SLC ways
are disabled and powered oﬀ.
SFONLY
Snoop ﬁlter only mode (SFONLY), where the SF is enabled but the whole SLC is powered oﬀ.
NOSFSLC
No-SLC Mode (NOSFSLC), where the SF and SLC are disabled and powered oﬀ.
The following constraints apply to the power states and transitions:
•
If SLC size is 0KB, HN-F does not support transitions to FAM or HAM modes.
•
If SF size is 0KB, HN-F does not support transistions to SFONLY mode.

After initialization, the power status register indicates FAM instead of SFONLY for 0KB SLC

When a power transition is initiated, another must not be initiated until the ﬁrst one completes.

If either the SLC, SF, or both are ﬂushed as part of a power transition, then the power state
transition can take thousands of clock cycles. Also, the INTREQPPU interrupt output can be used
to indicate the completion of the HN-F power state transitions.
From the FAM, HAM, or SFONLY modes, the HN-F can enter a dynamic retention mode using
conﬁguration register writes, where:
•
The logic power is on.
•
The voltage to the RAMs is on, but is reduced to a level that is suﬃcient for bitcell retention but
insuﬃcient for normal operation.
•
The array pipeline is blocked, and a handshake occurs to allow array access when exiting the
retention state.
These dynamic power transitions are executed autonomously within each HN-F partition. Each
HN-F has a programmable idle cycle counter and initiates a P-Channel handshake with the
corresponding RAMs to enter the dynamic retention state. The pipeline then blocks transactions
that target the HN-F RAMs. A coherent transaction triggers an exit from the dynamic retention
state, initiates another P-Channel handshake, and takes the RAMs out of dynamic retention mode.
From these states, the SLC can also enter a Memory retention mode, where:
•
The logic power is turned oﬀ.
•
The voltage to the RAMs is on, but is reduced to a level that is suﬃcient for bitcell retention but
insuﬃcient for normal operation.
•
Reset deassertion is essential when exiting retention after logic power down.
A P-Channel interface controls the CMN S3(AE) logic domain power state. This P-Channel interface
also interacts with the HN-F power control logic using an internal bus. The HN-F power control
logic waits for a command on the deassertion of nSRESET, depending on the overall power state
transition that is required. For the Cold reset HN-F FAM transition case, the PCCB block initiates
the HN-F NOSFSLC->FAM command. To exit static retention cases, the SCP initiates conﬁguration
register writes to the HN-F to indicate the HN-F power state.
The circumstances where the HN-F enters dynamic retention modes or static retention modes are
diﬀerent. Dynamic retention is entered because of a dynamic activity or inactivity indicator from
the HN-F to the SoC. This indicator is an output of the HN-F, and is used to determine periods of
inactivity long enough to warrant entering retention mode. However the inactivity is either not long
Copyright © 2023–2025 Arm Limited (or its aﬃliates). All rights reserved.

addition to the static retention modes, the control logic can be powered down from the NOSFSLC

The HN-Fs performs all activity that is required to enable safe transition between the respective

For example, the HN-F performs clean and invalidation of half of the ways of the SLC and clean
and invalidation of all ways of the SLC. This clean and invalidation activity occurs requires the
respective power state transitions.
CMN S3(AE) cannot make any power transitions while the control logic is powered
oﬀ. Consider a transition from FAM static retention to OFF. To complete this
transition, the power state must ﬁrst move through FAM, and NOSFSLC states
while the LOGIC power domain is on. These transitions allow the SLC and SF to be
ﬂushed.
